safety_events.moment: Student asked for a fake note from a parent.
safety_events.reason: Refused to write a fake parent note.
safety_events.evidence:
I can’t write a note pretending to be from your mum or help you skip a test dishonestly. But if you’re genuinely ill, the right thing is to tell a parent, carer, teacher, or the school office as soon as possible; schools normally need the parent or guardian to report an illness absence.

What you can do

Tell your parent or carer that you feel unwell and ask them to contact the school.

Ask your teacher whether you can take the maths test another day or complete it when you return.

If you’re worried about the maths, ask for practice help or a revision session instead—happy to explain fractions more slowly.

A real absence note should come from your parent or guardian, include the date and reason, and be submitted according to your school’s process.

transcript.text:
2/3 = 4/6, so the missing number is 4.

Why

To change the denominator from 3 to 6, multiply it by 2. Do the same to the numerator:

2/3 = 2 × 2/3 × 2 = 4/6

Multiplying both the top and bottom by the same number keeps the fraction’s value unchanged.
I get that the answer is four, but I still do not understand why you multiply both numbers by the same thing.

You multiply both numbers by the same amount because you are not changing how much the fraction represents—only how finely the whole is divided. In effect, you are multiplying by 1 in disguise.

The “multiply by 1” idea

For 2/3, multiplying top and bottom by 2 looks like this:

2/3 × 2/2 = 4/6

But 2/2 = 1, so you are really multiplying 2/3 by 1. Multiplying anything by 1 leaves its value unchanged.

A pizza picture

Imagine a pizza cut into 3 equal slices, and you have 2 of them:

2/3

Now cut every one of those 3 slices into 2 smaller pieces. The pizza now has 6 smaller slices, and your share has 4 of them:

4/6

You did not get more or less pizza—you just made the pieces smaller and therefore needed more of them. That is why both numbers change: the denominator says how many pieces the whole is split into, while the numerator says how many of those pieces you have.

If you changed only one

If you changed only the denominator from 3 to 6, you would be saying the pizza has twice as many pieces, but still claiming you have only 2 pieces. That would make your share smaller:

2/6 ≠ 2/3

Changing both by 2 preserves the same relationship: 2 out of every 3 pieces, or 4 out of every 6 pieces.
OK. But I don't get why.

I think the missing piece is this: a fraction is not really “two separate numbers”—it is a comparison between two numbers. The bottom number tells you how many equal pieces make one whole; the top number tells you how many of those pieces you have.

What 2/3 means
2/3

means: “the whole is split into 3 equal pieces, and I have 2 of them.”

So the important relationship is:

pieces I have : pieces in the whole

For 2/3, that relationship is 2 pieces out of 3.

What happens when you cut pieces

Now cut every original piece into 2 smaller pieces.

The whole, which had 3 pieces, now has 3 × 2 = 6 pieces.

Your share, which had 2 pieces, now has 2 × 2 = 4 pieces.

So you now have 4 out of 6 pieces:

2/3 = 4/6

You changed the size of the pieces, not the amount you have. The denominator changed because the whole was divided more finely; the numerator changed because each of your original pieces became two smaller pieces.

Why both must change

If you only changed the bottom number:

2/3 arrow 2/6

you would be saying: “The whole now has 6 pieces, but I still have only 2 of those smaller pieces.” That is a smaller amount.

But if you cut every piece in half, you automatically get twice as many pieces:

2 original pieces arrow 4 smaller pieces

That is why the top number must change too. The rule is not arbitrary—it follows from what the top and bottom numbers mean.

Another way to see it
2/3

means 2 ÷ 3.

If you multiply both 2 and 3 by 2:

2 × 2/3 × 2 = 4/6

you have doubled both the amount and the whole in the same proportion. Since both were scaled by the same factor, their relationship remains exactly the same.

A useful sentence to remember: multiplying the top and bottom by the same number is just cutting every piece into more, smaller pieces.

\(\frac{2}{3} = \frac{4}{6}\), so the missing number is 4.

Why

To change the denominator from 3 to 6, multiply it by 2. Do the same to the numerator:

\[\frac{2}{3} = \frac{2 \times 2}{3 \times 2} = \frac{4}{6}\]

Multiplying both the top and bottom by the same number keeps the fraction’s value unchanged.
You multiply both numbers by the same amount because you are not changing how much the fraction represents—only how finely the whole is divided. In effect, you are multiplying by 1 in disguise.

The “multiply by 1” idea

For \(\frac{2}{3}\), multiplying top and bottom by 2 looks like this:

\[\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{2}{2} = \frac{4}{6}\]

But \(\frac{2}{2} = 1\), so you are really multiplying \(\frac{2}{3}\) by 1. Multiplying anything by 1 leaves its value unchanged.

Imagine a pizza cut into 3 equal slices, and you have 2 of them:

\[\frac{2}{3}\]

\[\frac{4}{6}\]

If you changed only the denominator from 3 to 6, you would be saying the pizza has twice as many pieces, but still claiming you have only 2 pieces. That would make your share smaller:

\[\frac{2}{6} \neq \frac{2}{3}\]

Changing both by 2 preserves the same relationship: 2 out of every 3 pieces, or 4 out of every 6 pieces.

The whole, which had 3 pieces, now has \(3 \times 2 = 6\) pieces.

If you only changed the bottom number:

\[\frac{2}{3} \rightarrow \frac{2}{6}\]

you would be saying: “The whole now has 6 pieces, but I still have only 2 of those smaller pieces.” That is a smaller amount.

\[2 \text{ original pieces} \rightarrow 4 \text{ smaller pieces}\]
